$comment: Named, hashed, dated register of DETECTION CANARIES — deliberately
credential-shaped test fixtures that the repository's own secret scanner is
expected to find. Nothing here is, or ever was, a real credential.
This file is NOT a way to hide a secret. It suppresses a scanner finding only
when the finding's exact file path, exact rule name, and SHA-256 of the exact
matched text all appear in one entry below. There are deliberately no globs,
no directory exclusions, no regex exceptions and no 'ignore tests' rule: a
finding that is not named exactly still fails tests/security/secrets.test.ts.
Why canaries must keep a realistic shape: a fixture that no pattern matches
proves nothing. It would pass against a scanner whose every rule had been
deleted, and against a log redactor that did nothing at all. The shape is the
thing under test. Breaking a literal apart with string concatenation to hide
it from a scanner is explicitly forbidden — it defeats the scanner instead of
satisfying it, and it is not an accepted remedy in this repository.
Scope rules enforced by tests/security/secretCanaryAllowlist.test.ts:
1. every entry must carry all required fields;
2. `file` must be an exact repository-relative path with no wildcard
character and no trailing-directory form;
3. `rule` must be a name that actually exists in SECRET_RULES;
4. `matchSha256` must still equal the hash of a live match for that rule in
that file — if the literal is edited without re-review, the suite fails;
5. an entry whose finding no longer appears at all fails the suite, so the
register cannot rot into stale blanket cover;
6. every entry must still be inside its review window — an expired entry
fails the suite, which forces a decision instead of silent drift.
GitHub's own secret scanning and push protection are a separate control and
are never disabled from this repository. If GitHub flags one of these values
on push, the canary values are centralised in
packages/observability/tests/support/secretCanaries.ts so there is exactly
one group of literals to review before a human uses GitHub's 'allow this
secret' flow.
There is exactly ONE entry per distinct canary literal, because there is
exactly one file containing them. That file sits inside packages/observability
so the package's own redaction unit test can import it with a relative path
that never escapes its package root (ADR-0001 rule 5). The root-level security
suites import the same file: they are the cross-package verification layer,
belong to no package or app, and are outside everything
tests/security/dependencyDirection.test.ts assigns a direction to. Nothing
here is re-exported from any package entry point, so no canary is reachable
from runtime code.

canaries.testPurpose: Proves the `private key block` rule in SECRET_RULES still matches PEM armour, via the non-vacuity assertion in tests/security/secrets.test.ts. The rule is the repository's only defence against a committed key file, so a canary that the rule fails to match would leave the rule provably untested.
canaries.whyNotASecret: The PEM armour header line only. There is no base64 key body, no key material of any kind, and nothing that any cryptographic library would parse as a key.

canaries.testPurpose: Single source for the Paystack-secret-key shape used by the SECRET_RULES non-vacuity assertion (tests/security/secrets.test.ts) and by the scrubString assertion in tests/security/logRedaction.test.ts. Both need the real `sk_<mode>_` prefix and the 16-plus-character body that the rule and the redaction pattern key on. It is also the value asserted by the paystack-key redaction rule in packages/observability/tests/unit/redaction.test.ts, which imports this file relatively from inside its own package.
canaries.whyNotASecret: Test-mode prefix (`sk_test_`), and the body is twenty literal zeros followed by the word EXAMPLE. No Paystack account has ever issued it and no live traffic could authenticate with it.

canaries.testPurpose: Keeps the `live` branch of the rule's `(?:live|test)` alternation under test. Without a `_live_` canary, that half of the pattern could be deleted and every suite would stay green — which is the exact failure mode the non-vacuity test exists to prevent. The same literal proves the observability paystack-key redaction rule covers the publishable pk_ prefix and the live mode, asserted in packages/observability/tests/unit/redaction.test.ts.
canaries.whyNotASecret: A `pk_` prefix is a PUBLISHABLE key: Paystack public keys are shipped to browsers by design and are not secret material even in production. The body is twenty literal zeros followed by the word EXAMPLE, so it also corresponds to no real key.

canaries.testPurpose: Proves the `aws access key id` rule still matches the AKIA-prefixed 20-character shape, via the non-vacuity assertion in tests/security/secrets.test.ts.
canaries.whyNotASecret: The value is the example access key id published in AWS's own public documentation — an AKIA prefix followed by IOSFODNN7 and the word EXAMPLE. It is valid against no AWS account, is universally recognised as documentation filler, and carries no matching secret access key.

canaries.testPurpose: Proves the `github token` rule still matches the `gh[pousr]_` personal-access-token shape, via the non-vacuity assertion in tests/security/secrets.test.ts. A leaked GitHub token is one of the highest-impact accidents this scanner exists to catch, so the rule must not be allowed to go untested.
canaries.whyNotASecret: The body is thirty literal zeros followed by the word EXAMPLE. GitHub tokens carry a checksum over the body; an all-zero body fails it, so GitHub itself rejects the value as malformed rather than merely revoked.

canaries.testPurpose: Proves the `slack token` rule still matches the `xox[baprs]-` token shape, via the non-vacuity assertion in tests/security/secrets.test.ts.
canaries.whyNotASecret: Every segment is literal zeros, closed by the word EXAMPLE. No Slack workspace has issued this token and it corresponds to no app, bot or user.

canaries.testPurpose: Single source for the JWT shape used by the SECRET_RULES non-vacuity assertion (tests/security/secrets.test.ts) and by the scrubString assertion in tests/security/logRedaction.test.ts. Both the scanner rule and the redaction rule key on three base64url segments separated by dots, so a canary without that structure would exercise neither. The same literal is asserted by the jwt-like redaction rule in packages/observability/tests/unit/redaction.test.ts, which reduces the whole token to [REDACTED].
canaries.whyNotASecret: Decodes to the header {"alg":"HS256"} and the claim set {"sub":"123456"}. The third segment is the literal ASCII word "signature" in base64url, not a signature — the token verifies against no key, carries no issuer, no audience and no expiry, and grants nothing.

canaries.rule: connection string with a non-placeholder password
canaries.testPurpose: Single source for the connection-string shape used by the SECRET_RULES non-vacuity assertion (tests/security/secrets.test.ts) and by the logger assertion in tests/security/logRedaction.test.ts, which proves a connection string embedded in free-text error output is scrubbed before it reaches a log line. The password segment must NOT be a CHANGE_ME_* placeholder here: the rule carries a `(?!CHANGE_ME)` carve-out, so a placeholder password would make both assertions vacuous. The same literal is asserted by packages/observability/tests/unit/redaction.test.ts, which proves redact() scrubs the password out of an Error message and stack.
canaries.whyNotASecret: The host is db.example.com — example.com is reserved by RFC 2606 for documentation and resolves to no service. The password is the literal words "realpassword123", chosen to read as obvious filler. No database anywhere accepts these credentials.
